newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin says it has lifted main information taboo.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin says it has lifted main information taboo.

text.p: The Kremlin said on Monday that it had lifted the information taboo on President Boris Yeltsin's health, but it left several questions about his latest illness unanswered.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin, who is in hospital with pneumonia, had been instrumental in ending the Soviet-era habit of covering up leaders' illnesses.
He told a news conference to mark Russia's Media Day there had been progress in openness but sometimes the Kremlin's pronouncements on Yeltsin's health were over-optimistic.

"I think we've lifted the main taboo -- on the theme of the president's health," said Yastrzhembsky, who has been in the spotlight since the 65-year-old president was taken to hospital last week with what doctors said were signs of pneumonia.
"Maybe sometimes we are more optimistic than reality but maybe it's a question of Soviet traditions. We are historically optimistic," he said.

Yastrzhembsky, appointed last August, has been more forthcoming than his predecessors, but a long tradition of Kremlin cover-ups overshadows his reports on the heart and other health problems that have dogged Yeltsin in the past two years.

When Yeltsin disappeared from view during last year's presidential election, officials said at first it was a cold. Two months later, the surgeon chosen to lead a bypass operation on Yeltsin said he thought he had had a third heart attack.

Yastrzhembsky said on Monday that Yeltsin's condition -- which doctors are not linking to the November 5 operation -- was stable but gave no date for him to leave the Central Clinical Hospital where he was taken last Wednesday.
"I would not rush too much to release the president," he told reporters after the latest doctors' report.
He said that Yeltsin was well enough to work on documents but he did not know for how long each day.
He sidestepped a question on how serious the Kremlin considered the illness to be.
As for other aspects of the life of the Kremlin, Yastrzembsky said they should be subject to scrutiny, but within limits.

"One shouldn't take things to absurd lengths. The taking of state decisions should not look like an aquarium where one can go up and look at the fish moving around and the inner life of the aquarium," the spokesman said.
"There are some limitations which are linked mainly with common sense and the country's security interests," he said, adding that this was usual international practice.
Yastrzhembsky called Yeltsin's announcement in September that he was ill and needed heart surgery "historic".
"It was of course a very brave step which did a lot to create the favourable conditions for our work today," he said.

The Kremlin press service acts as a bridge between Yeltsin and the public, said Yastrzhembsky, adding that the new openness, which had been instituted since he took over and which he planned to build on further, worked both ways.
"We considered that the information which arrived on the president's desk in August was a long way from the real state of the press, of journalists' views," he said.
The media surveys were "too general, too wide of the mark, too smooth and too complimentary from the point of view of the real information that comes out in the media each day".
Now, he said, the press service did not hide unpleasant reports from Yeltsin.
